english_translation: My body feels tired and heavy, so I want to rest today.

dialogue.shona: Muviri wangu unonzwa kuremerwa saka ndiri kuda kuzorora nhasi.
dialogue.english: My body feels tired and heavy, so I want to rest today.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Muviri [in / singular viri] • wangu [wangu] • unonzwa [you nzwa] • kuremerwa [to / at remerwa] • saka [so / therefore] • ndiri [ndiri] • kuda [to / at da] • kuzorora [to / at zorora] • nhasi [today]

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unonzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unonzwa' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('wangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'wangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Listening to the Body ('Muviri Unonzwa Kuremerwa') & Rest
cultural_notes.content: In Shona, physical fatigue is vividly described as the body 'feeling weighed down' ('muviri unonzwa kuremerwa'), a signal to take a day of rest and recovery at home.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new polite request into English: 'Chimbomirira zvishoma pamusuwo.'
options: Come inside the house and sit on the chair.
Return home early before the sun sets.
Take your books and put them in the bag.
Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Chimbomirira' = 'Wait a little / for a moment right now', 'zvishoma' = 'a little', 'pamusuwo' = 'at the door'.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Shiri diki dziri kuimba pamusoro pemuti', what are the small birds doing?
options: Singing at the top of the tree
Looking for seeds in the field
active_exercises.correct_answer: Singing at the top of the tree
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shiri diki' = 'small birds', 'dziri kuimba' = 'are singing', 'pamusoro pemuti' = 'at the top of the tree'.
